On 1,756 tasks from nine comparison suites, Kairos solved more tasks at the full limits than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite. ★★★★ Notable: The authors select heterogeneous planning engines by task semantics and schedule them under one budget, reporting comparisons on 1,756 tasks, ablations, and a VAL cross-check.

entry.title: Gaussian approximation of smooth functions for logistic classification on curved data manifolds
entry.summary: High-Order Gaussian Approximation of Besov Functions on Manifolds arXiv · Oct 19, 2026This paper studies Gaussian kernel approximation and regularized logistic classification on a compact smooth manifold without boundary, measured by its intrinsic dimension. The authors build Gaussian approximants directly on the manifold, avoiding second-order saturation while keeping norm control tied to intrinsic dimension. They derive logistic excess-risk rates, and show that clipping predictions gives a faster rate whose exponent matches the minimax optimal squared-loss regression rate for bounded densities. ★★★★★ Notable: On compact manifolds, the authors report overcoming second-order saturation in Gaussian approximation for logistic classification, with intrinsic-dimension excess-risk rates and faster clipped rates.

entry.title: Why Howard's policy iteration can take exponentially long on deterministic decision problems
entry.summary: Policy Iteration Is Not Polynomial for Deterministic Markov Decision Processes: The Price of Algorithmic Anarchy arXiv · Oct 1, 2026The paper shows that Howard's policy iteration needs exponentially many iterations in the number of states for deterministic discounted and average-reward Markov decision processes, so it is not strongly polynomial. It proves that a Dantzig-style variant runs in strongly polynomial time on deterministic average-reward MDPs. Together with known results for Dantzig's rule on discounted MDPs, this establishes an exponential gap between the two methods. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show exponential lower bounds for Howard's policy iteration and a strongly polynomial Dantzig variant, establishing an exponential separation on deterministic MDPs.

entry.title: Neon-HTLC: Collateral-free hash time-locked contracts with logarithmic timeouts
entry.summary: Neon-HTLC: Collateral-Free HTLCs with Logarithmic Timeout IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper addresses the vulnerability of hashed time-lock contracts (HTLCs) to bribery attacks, where miners can be incentivized to censor honest transactions. It shows that existing incentive-compatible HTLCs must trade off between collateral and timeout, and proves this tradeoff holds for a generalized class called two-phase HTLCs, along with identifying optimal parameters. The authors propose Neon-HTLC, which removes the need for collateral by using a punishment that grows exponentially over time, so the timeout scales only logarithmically with payment amount. In their evaluation, a $100,000 payment is secured in 26 blocks with zero collateral, compared with 496 blocks and $5,000 collateral for He-HTLC. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose collateral-free, incentive-compatible HTLCs with logarithmic timeout, prove a tradeoff bound for two-phase HTLCs, and report comparisons with He-HTLC.

entry.title: Practical Key Collisions for Reduced-Round AES with Fixed Plaintext
entry.summary: Practical Fixed-Plaintext Key Collisions on Reduced-Round AES IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies finding different AES keys that produce the same ciphertext for a fixed all-zero plaintext, using reduced-round versions of AES. The result bears on key-committing security of AES-based authenticated encryption. The authors present practical collision attacks on 4-round AES-128, 7-round AES-256, and 6-round AES-192, the last one below the 2^64 birthday bound. They report experimental verification of all three attacks and provide a colliding key pair for each. ★★★★ Notable: The authors break fixed-plaintext non-linear cycles via linear elimination, reporting a practical one-block collision on 4-round AES-128 and attacks on 6- and 7-round variants.

entry.title: Computational Security Verification of Signal's Implementation with Owl
entry.summary: Compositional, Computational Security Verification of the Signal Implementation Under Fine-Grained Compromise with Owl IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper extends the Owl protocol-verification framework to give computational guarantees of fine-grained secrecy properties, such as forward secrecy and post-compromise security, for key-ratchet protocols. The authors apply Owl to Signal's entire two-party messaging protocol suite, building models and proving its core security properties. Owl-generated Rust libraries interoperate with and match the performance of Signal's open-source implementations. The authors also verify Signal's existing Rust implementation against the Owl-generated specifications. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a type-based model of key derivation chains and logical queries for fine-grained secrecy, applying Owl to Signal's two-party suite and reporting computational proofs plus Rust co

entry.title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the Random Oracle Model
entry.summary: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the ROM IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies hash-based vector commitments, where Merkle trees have long been the most efficient construction. In a Merkle tree, a verifier opens any bit with log n hash evaluations. The authors prove that, in the random oracle model, any vector commitment with deterministic verifiers needs Ω(log n) queries, so sublogarithmic verifier complexity is impossible. High-arity Merkle trees match this lower bound up to constant factors. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a tight Omega(log n) random-oracle lower bound on verifier hash queries for vector commitments, via a computational BKR-style lemma matched by high-arity Merkle trees.

entry.title: Reducing T gates in product formulas using LLM agent loops
entry.summary: Reducing T gates in product formulas with agent loops arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper uses the Nemotron 3.5 Lightning language model in a coding-agent loop to optimize product formulas for quantum phase estimation, aiming to lower the T-gate cost on fault-tolerant quantum computers. The resulting protocol, ELOTE, reduced the median and geometric-mean T95 cost by 85.35% and 84.82% across 115 molecular Hamiltonians while meeting chemical accuracy on the training set. A further optimized δ-ELOTE protocol lowered geometric-mean T95 by 58.90% relative to ELOTE for ten reaction energies while preserving chemical accuracy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use an LLM coding-agent loop to search product-formula structure and synthesis precision, yielding ELOTE; the report gives 85.35% median T95 reduction across 115 HamLib Hamiltonians, plus

entry.title: How Many Keys a Quantum Computer Must Break to Control a Proof-of-Stake Blockchain
entry.summary: How Many Keys Must a Quantum Computer Break to Take Over a Blockchain? A Quantum Nakamoto Coefficient for Fifteen Proof-of-Stake Networks arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper measures how many validator keys a quantum computer would need to break to take over the voting in fifteen proof-of-stake blockchains, defining a "quantum Nakamoto coefficient." Using live data collected on 15 November 2026, it reports the key counts needed to defeat security guarantees and gain full control. It also derives a formula showing how a 2025 Ethereum change that merged deposits into fewer keys sharply reduced the number of keys required. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a quantum Nakamoto coefficient, derive two formulas, and report checking them on live data from fifteen proof-of-stake networks.

entry.title: Sample Complexity of Quantum Function-State Tests for Monotonicity and Related Properties
entry.summary: Quantum Copy Complexity of Testing Monotonicity and Other Properties arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies how many copies of a quantum function state are needed to test whether a Boolean function is monotone. The authors give an improved tester with a better sample complexity upper bound than previously known, and prove the first nontrivial lower bounds for this task. The same framework also yields an Ω(n²) lower bound for testing union-closedness and 2-monotonicity. ★★★★ Notable: The authors improve the quantum function state monotonicity tester's sample complexity and give first nontrivial lower bounds, matching over a broad range of epsilon.

entry.title: When does a noisy Bell pair reach the Rains bound?
entry.summary: When does a noisy Bell pair attain the Rains bound? arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper studies two Bell-diagonal qubit states with the same singlet fraction and their achievable rates under operations that preserve the positive partial transpose. It shows that the Rains bound is reached only when one of the Bell probabilities is zero. Every mixed entangled isotropic state in any finite dimension lies strictly below its bound, implying the two-way quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel is below its relative-entropy bound. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show PPT-preserving attainable rates of Bell-diagonal states can differ, giving an iff condition for attaining the Rains bound. They report strict gaps for all mixed isotropic states and i

entry.title: Exact optimal covariance-based entanglement tests for thermal states of the XY spin chain
entry.summary: Structure-factor witnesses of thermal entanglement: exact optimal covariance criteria for the XY chain arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies entanglement in thermal equilibrium states of the spin-1/2 XY chain in a transverse field. Using a covariance-matrix criterion that requires only one- and two-spin correlations, the authors show that the optimal witness for thermal states is determined by the momentum minima of three static spin structure factors, which scattering experiments can access. These witnesses certify entanglement and bound entanglement measures up to temperatures of the order of the exchange coupling, including in states with no pairwise entanglement. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show the optimal covariance-criterion witness for thermal XY-chain states is set by momentum minima of three static structure factors, with small-chain comparisons reported.

entry.title: KnitNet: Learning to Search at Inference Time for Exact RNA Design
entry.summary: KnitNet: Learning to Search at Inference Time for Exact RNA Inverse Design arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces KnitNet, an inference-time scaling framework that refines RNA nucleotide sequences using verifier feedback so they fold into exactly the target structure. It infers nucleotide dependencies from mismatched folds and uses an online surrogate to predict promising edits, making search more informed and efficient. Across five secondary-structure benchmarks, it raises exact solve rates by an average of 21 percentage points while cutting time-to-solve by 70%. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose inference-time search learning from verifier feedback with an online surrogate; the abstract reports higher exact solve rates and lower time-to-solve on five secondary-structure be

entry.title: Keep or Roll Back? Out-of-Loop Judges for Self-Improving Robot Policies
entry.summary: Keep or Roll Back? Out-of-Loop Judges for Self-Improving VLA and End-to-End Embodied Policies arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces SealedLoop, an evaluation framework that adds a sealed judge outside the self-improvement loop, which the improving system cannot see or optimize against. A new policy is kept only when a sequential test on this sealed judge confirms a gain, with a bounded chance of keeping a worse one. Experiments on LIBERO manipulation, NAVSIM driving, and a real vehicle show that even accurate in-loop judges are not enough to decide whether a policy has improved. ★★★★ Notable: The authors add a sealed out-of-loop judge with a sequential test to decide policy retention, separating judge error from transfer gap, and report results on LIBERO, NAVSIM, and a real vehicle.

entry.title: Change detection guided by a visual example pair
entry.summary: Show Me the Change You Want: Visual Example-Guided Change Detection arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper proposes Visual Example-Guided Change Detection (VECD), where an unannotated before-and-after image pair serves as an example to locate the same kind of change in another image pair. No text, example masks, or test-time fine-tuning are required. The method is evaluated on EditCLEVR, MagicBrush, HumanEdit, and MaskEdit, showing cross-dataset generalization without fine-tuning. On attribute families withheld from paired training, it reaches 74.54% to 93.38% mIoU across four holdout settings. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose guiding change localization with an unannotated before-after pair as visual example, evaluated across four datasets with cross-dataset generalization and held-out attribute familie

entry.title: VAPOR: A training-free method that speeds up multimodal reasoning by reusing visual attention
entry.summary: VAPOR: Improving Multimodal Reasoning with Sparse Visual Updates arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces VAPOR, a training-free framework that speeds up multimodal large language models during extended reasoning. It reuses cached visual attention outputs across decoding steps and refreshes them only when needed, while keeping the full visual key-value cache available. Across eight image and four video reasoning benchmarks, VAPOR improves accuracy over dense attention on nearly all benchmarks and achieves 1.11-1.21x decoding speedups. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose training-free reuse and on-demand refresh of visual attention per head, reporting accuracy gains and 1.11-1.21x decoding speedups across eight image and four video benchmarks.

entry.title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs
entry.summary: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents FlashProve-Next, which produces zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual responses from closed-weight LLM APIs, letting clients verify that the advertised model, precision, and reasoning budget were used. The method works without modifying native serving and without revealing weights, hidden prompts, or activations. The paper reports Lean 4 mechanized soundness proofs and proving and verification timings on Qwen3 models. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose zero-knowledge-masked proofs for LLM API responses without changing native serving, mechanized in Lean 4 and tested on Qwen3 models.

entry.title: Improved quantum algorithms for the traveling salesman problem and related problems
entry.summary: Improved Quantum Algorithms for TSP and More arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a classic NP-hard optimization problem. This paper improves the best known quantum running time for TSP from O*(1.7274^n) to O*(1.70961^n). The method combines the Ambainis et al. framework with an extremal set-system approach, splitting the optimal tour into four consecutive subpaths and using amplitude amplification. The authors also give a new quantum space-time tradeoff for TSP and the same quantum upper bounds for several related problems. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine Grover search with extremal set systems, improving the quantum TSP exponent from 1.7274^n to 1.70961^n and giving a new space-time tradeoff.

entry.title: MOVR-SAR: A Multi-resolution Radar Image Matching Dataset for Orbit-crossing and View-variant Imaging
entry.summary: MOVR-SAR: A Multi-resolution SAR Registration Dataset under Orbit-crossing and View-variant Imaging Differences arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces MOVR-SAR, a dataset of 450,845 registered and quality-screened tile pairs from 2774 radar scene pairs captured by Capella, Umbra, Sentinel-1, and NISAR. It labels pairs by orbit direction, look side, and viewing-angle separation, enabling stratified evaluation of registration under different imaging geometries. Existing pretrained models perform poorly on high-resolution X-band imagery, while fine-tuning on MOVR-SAR substantially improves accuracy and reduces differences across platforms and geometry categories. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a multi-resolution SAR registration dataset with geometry-aware stratified evaluation; the abstract reports large AUC@5 gains after fine-tuning on Capella and Umbra.

entry.title: Node-private graph algorithms via stable degree-bounded projections
entry.summary: Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper introduces two tools for designing node-differentially private algorithms on graph data. The first is a randomized, nearly linear time graph projection that leaves graphs of maximum degree D unchanged, maps other graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree about D, and is stable under changing one node. The second is a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for total edge weight on bounded-weight graphs. The authors also show how to apply these methods to high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a nearly linear time node-stable graph projection and a deterministic Lipschitz extension, applying them to node-private vector summation and gradient descent.

entry.title: Recognizing fine-grained ego-vehicle maneuvers in driving videos
entry.summary: Fine-Grained Ego-Vehicle Action Recognition from Driving Video arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces EgoManeuver, a unified benchmark built from seven public driving datasets, with 16 lateral and 6 longitudinal actions. It contains 86.6K segments totaling 190.8 hours across 26 countries. The authors also propose DenseEgo, a video baseline that reports 82.7 lateral and 83.5 longitudinal mAP on the benchmark. ★★★★ Notable: The authors unify seven public driving datasets into a fine-grained ego-action benchmark and propose DenseEgo, reporting gains over the strongest existing video model.

entry.title: Small Leaks Sink Great Ships: Automated Analysis of Low-Entropy Key Protocols
entry.summary: Small Leaks Sink Great Ships: Automated Analysis of Protocols That Tolerate Low-Entropy Keys arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents a protocol-agnostic, automated symbolic method for analyzing protocols such as WPA2-PSK, BLE, and Bluetooth Classic that tolerate low-entropy keys, implemented as EntropyVerif, an extension of Tamarin. Using the tool, the authors rediscover the PMKID, KNOB, and Method Confusion attacks. They also report a new attack on Bluetooth Classic, the Unilateral Multi-Downgrade (UMD) attack, which reduces session-key recovery cost for devices using 128-bit keys from 2^128 to n·2^(128/n). ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a protocol-agnostic automated symbolic method for low-entropy keys and report a new BC downgrade attack reducing key recovery cost.

entry.title: DoseSteer: Steering diffusion-based radiotherapy dose predictors toward clinical targets at inference time
entry.summary: DoseSteer: Steering diffusion-based dose prediction models towards clinical targets via Dual-Response Guidance arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces DoseSteer, a method that adjusts frozen diffusion-based dose prediction models at inference time so their outputs better match specified structure-level clinical dose targets, without retraining. Its core algorithm, Dual-Response Guidance (DRG), probes how the model responds to perturbations in each structure's noisy dose and context, and jointly solves for per-structure steering strengths. Across five dataset-model configurations, DRG outperforms 12 training-free baselines, removing at least 97% of target error and reducing official dose error by 7.8% on average. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose training-free inference-time guidance (DRG) aligning diffusion dose predictions to structure-level targets, compared against 12 baselines across three architectures and datasets.

entry.title: AVERT: A Defense Against Visual Prompt Injection That Removes Injected Content Only When Answers Depend on It
entry.summary: AVERT: Anomalous Value Erasure with Response Testing against Visual Prompt Injection arXiv · Nov 25, 2026Vision language models can be hijacked by adversarially perturbed images that force attacker-chosen responses. This paper proposes AVERT, which identifies image feature directions that deviate most from clean-image statistics and projects them out, applying the removal only when an answer depends on those directions. Tested against white-box attacks on four VLMs and four injection benchmarks, AVERT reduces average attack success from 86-90% to at most 0.6% while keeping at least 96% of undefended utility. ★★★★ Notable: The authors project out anomalous directions only for answers that depend on them, reporting attack success below 0.6% across four VLMs and four injection benchmarks.

entry.title: Adversarial bandit convex optimization with improved regret of d^{3/2}√n
entry.summary: Adversarial Bandit Convex Optimization with d³/2√n Regret arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies adversarial bandit convex optimization, where a learner picks points in a convex body and observes only noisy convex loss values chosen by an adversary. It improves the best known regret bound from O~(d^{5/2}√n) to O~(d^{3/2}√n), matching the rate conjectured by Bubeck et al. (2017). The algorithm is an online Newton step with Gaussian exploration that uses unbiased estimates of the gradient and Hessian of the loss's Gaussian smoothing. ★★★★ Notable: The authors improve the regret bound for adversarial bandit convex optimization to d^{3/2}√n, matching a conjectured rate, using an online Newton step with unbiased Gaussian-smoothed gradient and Hess

entry.title: Going beyond welfarism: a more affordable proportional approval voting rule
entry.summary: Beyond the Limits of Welfarism: An Affordable Proportional Approval Voting Rule arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies multiwinner elections with approval ballots, extending Proportional Approval Voting (PAV) by allowing committees of varying size while penalizing larger ones. It proposes an exact rule and a polynomial-time local-search variant, both yielding outcomes that admit a priceable completion and, on laminar instances, a laminar-proportional one. The analysis uses two marginal stability conditions to derive welfare and coverage guarantees and improves the best known lower bound on the utilitarian ratio of standard PAV. ★★★★ Notable: The authors go beyond welfarism with variable-size committees and penalties, obtaining priceable and laminar-proportional guarantees and improving PAV's utilitarian ratio lower bound.

entry.title: PRECEPT: Coding Agents Learning to Stay Secure Across Sessions
entry.summary: PRECEPT: Security Self-Improvement of Coding Agents via Evolving Principles arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper finds that AI coding agents can fix a security vulnerability when shown the failing test, yet often reintroduce the same vulnerability class in later sessions, at about the same rate as agents that never saw it. Neither storing the repair nor giving general secure coding principles closed this gap. The authors present PRECEPT, a library that starts from authoritative secure coding principles and revises them using the agent's own failures, keeping only revisions that improve security without substantially hurting functional success. On task families unseen during evolution, its weakest agent reached 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent (81.9%) and the strongest baseline (87.7%). ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce security self-improvement and an evolving principle library that retains fixes across sessions, reporting comparisons over 14 task sequences and unseen task families.

entry.title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the Random Oracle Model
entry.summary: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the ROM arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper studies hash-based vector commitments, where a verifier opens a bit using hash evaluations. It proves that in the random oracle model, any such scheme with deterministic verifiers needs a logarithmic number of hash queries, so sublogarithmic verifier complexity is impossible. High-arity Merkle trees match this bound up to constant factors. The proof relies on a disjoint product lemma, a computational analog of the BKR inequality. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a tight Ω(log n) verifier query lower bound for vector commitments in the random oracle model, matched by high-arity Merkle trees, via a disjoint product lemma.

entry.title: A benchmark testing AI models' ability to find new security flaws in Windows kernel binaries.
entry.summary: Benchmarking Open-Ended Vulnerability Discovery in Windows Kernel Binaries arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces DeepBinary, the first comprehensive benchmark for open-ended vulnerability discovery in closed-source Windows kernel binaries. Agents analyze target binaries using a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated virtual machines, reporting each vulnerability with a crashing proof of concept. Across 12 target binaries, the evaluated models and coding agents discovered over 200 vulnerabilities, including 146 distinct previously unknown ones. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first open-ended vulnerability discovery benchmark for Windows kernel binaries, reporting over 200 findings on 12 binaries, including 146 unknown ones.

entry.title: SplatWAM: Real-time 3D world model that predicts scene changes using 3D Gaussians
entry.summary: SplatWAM: Splatting World Action Models for Real-Time 3D Imagination arXiv · Nov 25, 2026SplatWAM is a generative world model that predicts how a 3D scene changes in response to actions, working directly on compact 3D Gaussian primitives instead of pixels or latent features. Its tokenizer encodes a variable number of unposed views into a fixed set of Gaussian tokens, and its dynamics model predicts future Gaussian states in one forward pass per action. The authors also add SplatWAM-P, a lightweight flow-matching policy head. On OGBench Scene, the model renders novel views about 12 times faster than video world models with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR, and on LIBERO its roughly 1B-parameter model outperforms WorldVLA and OpenVLA. ★★★★ Notable: The authors learn action-conditioned dynamics directly over 3D Gaussian primitives and add a flow-matching policy head. They report rendering speed and PSNR gains on OGBench Scene and LIBERO compariso

entry.title: Fast training of muscle-driven full-body motion tracking using a differentiable world model
entry.summary: Fast Muscle-Driven Whole-Body Motion Tracking with a Differentiable World Model arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper extends SuperMimic, a method that trains motion tracking policies by backpropagating through a learned world model, to full-body musculoskeletal models with 700 and 354 muscles. The authors modify the training recipe for muscle-driven control, which speeds up training on a single RTX 5090 GPU by a large factor compared with the published hyperparameters. They also report that refining actions through the world model at test time further reduces position error. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend SuperMimic to 700- and 354-muscle models with Beta noise and other changes; the abstract reports 37x faster training on MS-Human-700 with ablations.

entry.title: Recovering Key Reference Details While Transferring Only Reliable Content for Precise Reference-Based Super-Resolution
entry.summary: Recovering What Matters, Transferring Only What Is Reliable: Toward Precise Reference-Based Super-Resolution arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents PreciseRef, a generative framework for reference-based super-resolution that aims to faithfully recover reference-specific details such as text, codes, and identity cues while avoiding unreliable information transfer. Its core components are Asymmetric Twin-Attention (ATA) for fine-grained reference retrieval and Dual-Scale Reference Gating (DRG), which combines semantic relevance and bidirectional consistency gating. The authors also introduce the VeriRef benchmark, reporting 85.6% character accuracy and 76.3% exact code decoding, and state-of-the-art perceptual quality on CUFED5 and WR-SR. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose asymmetric twin-attention and dual-scale reference gating for precise reference recovery; the abstract reports 85.6% character accuracy on their VeriRef benchmark plus CUFED5 and W

entry.title: Centered Kernel Distance: a dimension-free error bound for comparing neural representations
entry.summary: Centered Kernel Distance: Dimension-Free Error Bounds for Comparing Neural Representations arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies the estimation error of representational similarity measures such as CKA and RSA. It introduces the Centered Kernel Distance (CKD), the metric counterpart of these measures, and shows that CKD has an unbiased estimator while CKA and several other popular measures do not. Under mild assumptions, the CKD estimation error decays in proportion to 1/M + 1/N and does not depend on the dimensionality of the experimental conditions space. The results are checked on random shallow networks, trained networks, and macaque visual cortex data. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose centered kernel distance, prove an unbiased estimator and a dimension-free error bound, and verify it on random networks, trained networks and macaque data.

entry.title: WADJET: Authorizing and Dispatching Whole Jobs to Keep FPGA Accelerator Execution Trustworthy
entry.summary: WADJET: Whole-Job Authorization and Dispatch for Job Execution Trust on FPGA System-on-Chip Accelerators arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper presents WADJET, an FPGA logic gate that combines exclusive access to an accelerator, whole-job verification before any release, and a record of used approvals. A separate authority encrypts and authenticates each approved job with a sequence number using Ascon-AEAD128, and the gate accepts only newer sequence numbers and writes the registers of an unmodified accelerator itself. On a Zynq-7020 running a language model, it released all 21,000 approved jobs and none of 14,700 altered or repeated jobs. It uses about a third of the lookup tables of ShEF's register protection and adds about ten microseconds to job startup. ★★★★ Notable: The authors merge access control, whole-job verification, and replay rejection into one FPGA hardware gate, reporting tests on Zynq-7020 with about 35,700 jobs and a comparison against ShEF.

entry.title: What RL Post-Training Teaches Text-to-Image Models: A Skill-by-Skill Look at Flow-GRPO
entry.summary: What Does RL Post-Training Teach Text-to-Image Models? A Skill-Wise Analysis of Flow-GRPO arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines where the gains from reinforcement learning post-training (Flow-GRPO) on text-to-image flow models come from. Measuring pass@k per skill on prompts unseen in training, the authors find that for most skills the training mainly sharpens outcomes the base model already produced. For spatial relations, however, it unlocks abilities the base model rarely reached, and the paper offers an account explaining both patterns. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors decompose Flow-GRPO gains by skill, separating sharpening from unlocking via pass@k on GenEval, and test their mechanism with controlled training holding out object classes.

entry.title: Building a Unified Inline Code Editing Model for GitHub Copilot
entry.summary: Building a Unified Inline Code Editing Model for GitHub Copilot arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents a single model that predicts code completions, nearby edits, and long-distance edits in one output format of anchored diff patches. It is trained in two phases using multi-edit data synthesized from single-edit data and a binary LLM-graded reward. In controlled online A/B tests in GitHub Copilot, the first phase cut time to display by 6.77% and output tokens by 58.93%, and the second phase cut dismissed suggestions per user by 10.06%. ★★★★ Notable: The authors unify next-edit, long-distance edit, and completion prediction into one anchored diff output, reporting 6.77% lower display time and 58.93% fewer output tokens in Copilot A/B tests.

entry.title: Verifying Proof Depth: Shortcut-Free Logic Reasoning Data
entry.summary: Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data arXiv · Nov 25, 2026Procedurally generated logic problems set difficulty by planting a proof of a chosen depth, but a problem may also have shorter proofs. This work computes, for each problem and a given set of inference rules, the steps every proof must take, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs, and the indispensable premises, and exports certificates that an independent checker verifies. Audits of eight datasets find some depths are forced, some problems labelled depth 5 need about two specific rule applications, and some answers need no particular step. The authors also construct problems whose every proof has a requested structure, and report that mixtures of certified problem types train Qwen3 models (0.6B to 8B) better than FLDx2-style derivation data at equal size. ★★★★ Notable: The authors audit proof depth via certificates across eight datasets, build shortcut-free problems, and report better transfer for Qwen3 models.

entry.title: CoSMo: A compact spectral code for body motion in video
entry.summary: CoSMo: A Compact Spectral Space of Body Motion in Video arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces CoSMo, a compact spectral space in which each body motion in a video is represented by a single 384-number code. The encoder captures how DINOv2 features change over time using a discrete cosine transform, allowing codes to be compared, blended, and transferred to new subjects without training. Compared with DisMo, FlexiAct, and a text-prompt baseline, the authors report more faithful motion transfer and more compact codes, and users ranked CoSMo first more often. ★★★★ Notable: The authors compress DINOv2 feature changes into a 384-dimensional DCT code enabling training-free comparison, blending, and transfer; they report gains over DisMo and FlexiAct on unseen videos and ge

entry.title: Optimal error bounds and exponents for universal randomness extraction against quantum side information
entry.summary: Sharp one-shot bounds and optimal exponents of universal randomness extraction arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies randomness extraction against quantum side information (privacy amplification) by relating it to hypothesis testing with quadratic constraints. It precisely determines the optimal scaling of the error of quantum privacy amplification in several regimes, using the standard trace-distance security criterion and focusing on universal hash function classes. The authors give one-shot converse bounds, establish the asymptotic i.i.d. error exponent of universal randomness extraction, and derive the exact strong converse exponent for 2-universal hash functions. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors relate privacy amplification to quadratically constrained hypothesis testing, giving optimal error scalings and tight strong converse exponents up to constant factors.

entry.title: Faster, scalable abstract interpretation for verifying deep neural networks (Scepter)
entry.summary: Fast and Scalable Abstract Interpretation for Deep Neural Networks arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents Scepter, a framework that specializes abstract interpreters for deep neural networks by separating structural computation from numerical evaluation and generating reusable tensor programs. The authors prove it computes the same bounds as the general interpreter in exact arithmetic. Across eight analyses and 44 DNNs, Scepter handles networks with up to 153x more neurons than baselines and achieves 11.9x to 44.4x geometric-mean GPU speedups over Neuton. ★★★★ Notable: The authors specialize DNN abstract interpreters via structural semantics into reusable tensor programs, reporting GPU speedups and memory reductions across eight analyses and 44 networks.

entry.title: Anti-AI in the Wild: A measurement study of online conflict over generative AI
entry.summary: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. The authors collected 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities and identified 3,312 anti-AI actions. They found 30.0% of posts in conflict-focused communities are toxic, compared with 4.4% in general AI communities. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first measurement of generative AI online conflict from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions, tracing tool outputs into Common Crawl and FineWeb across 931,640 posts.

entry.title: Typical Angina Reversed: A Documentation Error in UCI Heart Disease Data
entry.summary: Typical Angina, Reversed: A Long-Standing Documentation Error in the UCI Heart Disease Data arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper reports that the chest-pain variable in the widely used UCI Heart Disease machine-learning dataset is coded in reverse of its documentation. Records documented as "asymptomatic" (4) actually mark patients with typical angina, while "typical angina" (1) marks patients with almost none of its classical features. The authors support this with the 1986 Cleveland study's results and data from Budapest, Switzerland and Long Beach. They also show that interpretations and zero-shot language-model classifiers using the documented labels are misled. ★★★★ Notable: The authors find the UCI Heart Disease chest-pain codes are reversed relative to documentation, confirmed by reproducing a 1986 Cleveland study and by feature co-occurrence checks, with audits and lan

entry.title: Show Your Work: Can Small Open Models Read SEC Filings with Evidence a Machine Can Check?
entry.summary: Show Your Work: Can Small Open Models Read SEC Filings with Evidence a Machine Can Check? arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper asks whether small open language models that run on one consumer GPU can extract numbers from SEC filings and provide checkable evidence, namely the page and a verbatim quote containing the number. The authors introduce Filing-Evidence, a benchmark of 1,000 questions over 90 recent 10-K and 10-Q filings from 45 US companies, with answer keys taken from inline XBRL tags. Ten instruct models were tested in plain, check-and-retry, and reasoning setups, and the study finds that some wrong answers still pass the automatic checker. ★★★★ Notable: The authors evaluate ten 7-21B open models on a 1,000-question SEC filing benchmark, using machine-checkable page and quote evidence and analyzing wrong answers that still pass checks.

entry.title: Wavelet determinantal samplers with regularity-adaptive optimal approximation rates
entry.summary: Sampling with graph wavelet kernels: optimality and adaptivity to regularity and geometry arXiv · Nov 23, 2026The paper constructs wavelet-based determinantal samplers on manifolds and geometric graphs whose approximation rates adapt to the regularity of the observable. On an m-dimensional Riemannian manifold, linear statistics of s-Hölder and H^s observables achieve variance reduction of order n^{1-2s/m}. These samplers yield unbiased quadrature rules with root mean square error O(n^{-1/2-s/m}), matching the classical optimal randomized integration exponent. The authors also develop analogous samplers for point clouds on ε-graphs and symmetric k-nearest-neighbour graphs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct wavelet determinantal samplers whose variance reduction adapts to regularity, yielding unbiased quadrature matching the classical optimal exponent.

entry.title: Toward an ICU Patient Digital Twin: Forecasting and Treatment Response with a Generative Event Model
entry.summary: TWICE: Toward a digital twin of ICU patients with a generative event model for forecasting trajectories and simulating treatment response arXiv · Nov 20, 2026The paper presents TWICE, a 79-million-parameter decoder-only transformer trained on intensive care unit records from one academic health system to continue patients' electronic health records. Without task-specific training, it reads 19 clinical outcomes from 50 simulated futures and reaches a mean AUROC of 0.836, matching the best of 144 supervised configurations (0.834). The authors present the model as a step toward a digital twin of the ICU patient. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a generative event model as an ICU digital twin, reporting it matches the best of 144 supervised configurations on 19 outcomes without task-specific training.

entry.title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor and Its Closed-Loop Cost
entry.summary: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed-Loop Cost arXiv · Nov 13, 2026This paper studies how robot imitation policies trained on noisy object positions discount the noisy readings. The authors show that a trained policy blends its own proprioceptive state with the reading using a weight determined by reading noise and the learner's anchor error variance, and a pre-measured variance predicted ten held-out sensitivities with much lower error than classical errors-in-variables regression. Under closed-loop deployment, sensitivity to a persistent offset exceeded this weight, and lower weights predicted lower success, which a prospective test confirmed for diffusion policies. All results come from simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a predictive law for how imitation policies weight noisy object readings against proprioceptive anchors, reporting preregistered tests in simulation.

entry.title: VisionQ: A Benchmark for Vision-Language Models Judging Qualitative Computer Vision Results
entry.summary: VisionQ: Benchmarking VLM Judges on Criterion-Specific Comparisons of Computer Vision Method Outputs arXiv · Oct 1, 2026This paper introduces VisionQ, a benchmark built from peer-reviewed CVPR and ICCV comparison figures, testing whether vision-language models can pick the better output according to a named visual criterion. It includes 1,409 papers, 3,911 hand-annotated data points, a 51-leaf taxonomy of visual criteria, and a fine-tuned judge model called VisionQ-Judge. Evaluating 20 models, the strongest reaches only 63.1% accuracy against a 32.2% chance baseline, and reliability varies sharply across criteria.</summary> ★★★★ Notable: Proposes VisionQ, a criterion-conditioned VLM judging benchmark built from 1,409 CVPR/ICCV papers and 3,911 annotations; the authors report the strongest of 20 judges reaches 63.1% accuracy against 32

entry.title: BioLoom: Scaling Biomedical Vision-Language Models Using Scientific Article Structure
entry.summary: BioLoom: Scaling Biomedical Vision-Language Models by Learning from the Structure of Scientific Articles arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper proposes BioLoom, a method that improves biomedical vision-language contrastive pretraining by using structural relationships among figures, panels, captions, and article text. The authors build Loom52M, a dataset of 52.4 million image-text pairs. BioLoom (DFN-2B) reaches 56.82% domain-balanced mean accuracy across 67 zero-shot classification tasks, compared with 48.77% for MedPMC-CLIP. It also reports higher bidirectional mean Recall@1 than the strongest baselines on BioLoomBench and BioMedFlickr. ★★★★ Notable: The authors add structural article relations, such as related panels in one figure, to contrastive training and build the 52.4M-pair Loom52M dataset. The abstract reports BioLoom at 56.82% domain-bala

entry.title: Improved Bounds for Downward-Closed Delegation
entry.summary: Improved Downward-Closed Delegation Bounds arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper studies delegated choice under a downward-closed feasibility constraint, where principal and agent values may be correlated across items but items are independent. The authors give a deterministic, agent-oblivious menu that guarantees the principal more than 29/70 (about 0.41429) of the expected offline optimum under every best response, including ties resolved against the principal. The previous best guarantee for this setting was 0.1098. ★★★★ Notable: For downward-closed delegation, the authors give a deterministic menu guaranteeing the principal over 29/70 of the expected offline optimum, improving the prior 0.1098, and report several upper bounds

entry.title: Low-degree torus approximations of the AND function and ACC⁰ circuits
entry.summary: Low-Degree Torus Approximations of the AND Function and mathsfACC⁰ Circuits arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper studies approximating Boolean functions by torus polynomials, real polynomials evaluated modulo one. It shows that the AND function has an ε-approximating torus polynomial of degree O(log(n/ε)), improving prior bounds. It also gives improved degree bounds for Boolean functions computed by depth-d, size-s AC⁰[m] circuits. The authors further prove that periodic Fourier representations and low-degree torus approximations are equivalent. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors improve the torus-polynomial approximation degree for AND from O(log²(n/ε)) to O(log(n/ε)), give an improved bound for AC^0[m] circuits, and show that periodic Fourier representations and

entry.title: What a skill vocabulary costs: a closed-loop breakdown of demonstrated motions
entry.summary: What Does a Skill Vocabulary Cost? A Closed-Loop Decomposition over Demonstrated Motions arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper introduces Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ), which places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy by replacing each predicted action chunk with its nearest library element and correcting it within a bound, without training parameters. Tested across six architectures, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original. On LIBERO-90, the authors report that quantization costs nothing, skill choice costs at most 2 points, and the selectors' own placement and correction account for most of the remaining gap. ★★★★ Notable: The authors place a demonstrated-motion library after a trained policy, enabling closed-loop attribution; results reported on LIBERO-90 across six architectures including a 7B VLA.

entry.title: Anomalous front spreading in quantum many-body transport with memory-dependent resetting
entry.summary: Anomalous front propagation in many-body quantum transport with memory-dependent resetting arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces an exactly solvable framework for non-Markovian quantum many-body dynamics based on stochastic resetting with memory, applicable to arbitrary time-independent Hamiltonians including interacting systems. The authors study domain-wall melting in a one-dimensional chain of noninteracting fermions, deriving exact analytical results for the density profile, front edge structure, extreme-value statistics of the rightmost fermion, and integrated current. They find that memory turns ballistic transport into logarithmically slow propagation, with the front edge broadening as √(ln t) and extreme-value statistics changing from Tracy–Widom to Gaussian. The mean and variance of the integrated current both grow logarithmically in time, and numerical simulations agree well with the predictions. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce an exactly solvable memory-dependent resetting framework, derive analytic results for free-fermion domain-wall melting, and compare them with numerical simulations.

entry.title: Classical method for simulating fermion observables under particle-number-conserving quantum operations
entry.summary: Dirac Propagation for Simulating Fermionic Observables under Particle-Number-Conserving Unitaries arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces Dirac propagation, a classical method for simulating local observables in fermionic systems under particle-number-conserving unitary operations. The authors show that operator strings whose weight exceeds the total particle number can be discarded without error in the final expectation value. This exact cutoff keeps the number of retained strings polynomial in the number of modes at fixed particle number, including for interacting dynamics. The framework also supports simulating fermionic many-body dynamics and classically benchmarking fermionic quantum circuits. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce an exact operator-string cutoff at total particle number, bounding retained strings polynomially in modes, with explicit interacting-gate expressions for classical fermionic simu

entry.title: GHZ states of unbounded dimension from fixed-order multiphoton sources
entry.summary: Unbounded GHZ dimension from fixed-order multiphoton sources arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies the local dimension of GHZ states created by selecting events with exactly one photon in each output path. For two-photon sources the maximum local dimension is 2 for every even number of paths greater than 4. The authors show that three-photon sources can instead produce GHZ states of arbitrarily large local dimension. The proof models each source's three paths as an edge of a 3-uniform hypergraph, so accepted emission patterns correspond to perfect matchings, and the construction extends to r-uniform hypergraphs for any fixed r≥3. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show three-photon sources yield arbitrarily large local-dimension GHZ states via hypergraphs with many edge-disjoint perfect matchings, generalized to r-uniform hypergraphs.

entry.title: Optimal Trace Distance Estimation: a method for measuring how different two quantum states are, using the fewest samples possible.
entry.summary: Optimal Trace Distance Estimation arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents a trace distance estimator with optimal sample complexity for two unknown d-dimensional quantum states. It combines quantum tomography with polynomial approximation, using variance bounds derived from quantum Fourier analysis. The sample complexity matches the lower bound given by Wang (2026). ★★★★ Notable: The authors report an estimator matching the known lower bound of Wang (2026), combining tomography, polynomial approximation, and quantum Fourier analysis variance bounds.

entry.title: Second-order limits on quantum and private communication over erasure channels
entry.summary: Second-order asymptotics for the quantum and private capacities of the erasure channel arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper studies how much quantum or secret classical information an erasure channel can carry in finite blocks, where the channel either delivers a quantum system or signals that it was lost. It determines the optimal second-order coding rates for fixed infidelity, with a square-root correction term. The result covers entanglement transmission, entanglement generation, and private classical communication, with matching upper and lower bounds. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give matching second-order upper bounds for erasure-channel quantum and private capacities at every fixed infidelity, and show the privacy criterion affects the second-order term.

entry.title: Universal state merging for nearly i.i.d. quantum states
entry.summary: Universal state merging for almost i.i.d. states arXiv · Nov 24, 2026Quantum state merging transfers one party's share of a bipartite quantum state to another party while preserving its joint state with a purifying reference. For exactly i.i.d. copies, the optimal asymptotic net entanglement cost is S(A|B) ebits per pair. The paper shows this cost remains achievable under deviations from exact i.i.d. structure. A single sequence of one-way LOCC protocols, depending only on the state and a rate R above S(A|B), merges weakly almost i.i.d. sources with vanishing error. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show one LOCC merging protocol family achieves optimal S(A|B) cost universally over weakly almost i.i.d. sources, including Wasserstein and MSR subclasses.

entry.title: Envy-free cake division among five people
entry.summary: Envy-Free Cake-Cutting for Five Agents arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies envy-free cake-cutting, where a divisible resource is split among agents with different preferences so that no agent prefers another's piece. The authors develop a simpler approach that gives an efficient algorithm for five agents, producing a connected ε-envy-free division using O(log^3(1/ε)) queries. They also provide a new existence proof for the five-agent case that relies only on the intermediate value theorem. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a simpler approach giving a polylogarithmic-query connected envy-free algorithm for five agents, with an existence proof using only the intermediate value theorem.

entry.title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
entry.summary: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies how to distill long-horizon agent behavior from a stronger teacher model into a smaller student without access to the teacher's hidden chain-of-thought. The student is trained on the teacher's actions with its reasoning block left empty, plus a KL loss on its own generations to limit drift. The authors also introduce CoT-Proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning, and report higher task success on AppWorld and SWE-bench Verified. ★★★★ Notable: The authors distill long-horizon policies from teacher actions alone, report cross-format transfer, and show large gains on AppWorld and SWE-bench.

entry.title: Classical algorithms for sparse random Hamiltonians using free probability
entry.summary: Classical algorithms for sparse random Hamiltonians via free probability arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper designs a classical algorithm for sparse random non-local Hamiltonians that accurately computes spectral fluctuations, thermal values, and time-ordered and out-of-time-order correlation functions. For any subexponential precision ε, the algorithm runs in time (1/ε)^{2+o(1)}, nearly identical to a quantum simulation. It first computes the model's mean behavior, then applies a short hierarchy of instance-dependent corrections that use free probability theory to predict long-time behavior from short-time data. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use free probability to design a classical algorithm for sparse random Hamiltonians, reporting near-quantum runtime for spectra, thermal values and correlators at late times.

entry.title: RenGen: Image generation that uses as many tokens as a scene needs
entry.summary: RenGen: Generating Images with as Many Tokens as the Scene Needs arXiv · Nov 24, 2026RenGen is a latent diffusion model that generates images using region tokens instead of fixed grids of patch tokens, so simple scenes need fewer tokens and complex scenes need more. Each token covers a region of varying shape and position, and the number of anchor points at sampling time sets the balance between scene complexity and compute. On ImageNet 256×256 it reaches a gFID of 1.34 with 88 tokens per image on average, the best among methods that vary token count. It approaches the quality of the patch-based RAEv2 at 2.5 times lower latency. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use region tokens from a pretrained encoder so token count varies with scene complexity; on ImageNet 256 they report gFID 1.34 with 88 tokens on average.

entry.title: Breaking the Square-Root Barrier for Linear Swap Regret in Polyhedral Games
entry.summary: Breaking the Square-Root Barrier for Linear Swap Regret in Polyhedral Games arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies linear swap regret in self-play games, measuring cumulative regret against all affine self-maps of each player's strategy polytope. For compact polytopes defined by linear inequalities, the authors present a deterministic uncoupled dynamic with regret scaling as a polynomial in the game's description length times T to the 1/3 power, independent of the number of vertices. For perfect-recall n-player extensive-form games, they achieve logarithmic regret against all linear deviations, extending prior logarithmic trigger-regret results. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report breaking the square-root barrier for linear swap regret, achieving T^{1/3} on polytopes and logarithmic regret in extensive-form games.

entry.title: Reliability limits of error-correcting output codes with noisy binary classifiers
entry.summary: The Reliability Function of Error-Correcting Output Codes with Noisy Binary Classifiers arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies error-correcting output codes (ECOC), which build a multi-class classifier from binary classifiers. It analyzes the excess error rate relative to the Bayes (MAP) classifier when each binary classifier's log-odds are corrupted by Gaussian noise, deriving upper and lower bounds. The authors show that a large Hamming distance is both necessary and sufficient for reducing the excess error rate, and that for n-vs-rest codes the reliability function is determined in closed form. Experiments on ResNet-50 features for CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-1k are also reported. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive upper and lower bounds on ECOC excess error under noisy log-odds, fixing the reliability exponent for n-vs-rest codes, and report checks on semi-synthetic and ResNet-50 CIFAR and Im

entry.title: Local indices alone are insufficient: synchrony and global information in bandit algorithms
entry.summary: Local Indices Are Not Enough: Synchrony and Global Information in Bandit Algorithms arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies bandit algorithms that update an arm's index only when that arm is pulled, using only its own reward history and a local randomness budget. The authors prove that no such asynchronous local index algorithm can achieve O(log T) regret across all bandit instances. For synchronous local algorithms like Thompson Sampling, they show that a locally determined randomness budget per arm is enough to keep O(log T) regret, indicating synchrony is essential to Thompson Sampling's optimality. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove asynchronous local index bandit algorithms cannot achieve O(log T) regret and characterise a sub-polynomial achievable regime.

entry.title: (1-ε)-MMS Allocations: Near-Fair Division of Indivisible Items
entry.summary: (1-ǎrepsilon)-MMS Allocations arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies maximin share (MMS) allocations, a fairness criterion, of m indivisible items among n agents with additive valuations. The authors prove that for both goods and chores, the optimal MMS approximation factor converges to 1 as n grows. For fixed ε and sufficiently large n, they give polynomial-time algorithms computing a (1-ε)-MMS allocation for goods and a (1+ε)-MMS allocation for chores. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show the optimal MMS approximation factor tends to 1 as agents grow, with polynomial-time algorithms for goods and chores.

entry.title: Approximate maximin share (MMS) fair allocation with many agents
entry.summary: Approximate MMS allocations for large number of agents arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies allocating indivisible items to agents with non-negative additive valuations, using the maximin share (MMS) fairness benchmark. It proves that for every ρ<1 there is an n_ρ such that any instance with at least n_ρ agents admits a ρ-MMS allocation. This result was previously posed as a conjecture by the authors and had been shown only when the number of items is at most (2−ε)n. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove that for enough agents a rho-MMS allocation always exists, resolving a conjecture, using new block-matching techniques.

entry.title: Worth the Wait? Response Time, Streaming and Judgments of AI Chatbot Answers
entry.summary: Worth the Wait? How Response Time and Streaming Shape Judgments of Generative AI Answers and Chatbot Engagement arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines how the speed and display style of answers from LLM chatbots affect user judgments. It analyzes blind votes from the French government chatbot arena compar:IA, slower streamed answers caused by provider congestion, and everyday ChatGPT replies in the WildChat dataset. The same text won more votes when streamed as it was written than when shown at once, and slower replies made users less likely to ask follow-up questions. ★★★★ Notable: The authors separate answer delivery (streaming versus cached replay) from blind votes, reporting three natural-data tests; streamed text won more votes and delays reduced follow-up questions.

entry.title: Spectrify: A Framework for Generating Hyperspectral Images from Computer Graphics
entry.summary: Spectrify: Framework for Hyperspectral Image Generation Using Computer Graphics arXiv · Nov 25, 2026Hyperspectral images capture the full light spectrum at each pixel, but real ones are costly to collect and datasets are small. This paper presents Spectrify, which converts 3D scene datasets into hyperspectral images using material-labeled reflectance spectra and wavelength-by-wavelength path tracing in Mitsuba 3. A reconstruction network trained only on these synthetic images generalizes better to most unseen real datasets than networks trained on the largest real datasets. The authors release 4,500 rendered images, the code, and the reflectance library. ★★★★ Notable: The authors render 4,500 hyperspectral images with material-based measured spectra, report gains in hyperspectral reconstruction transfer and color constancy, and release code and data.

entry.title: E-MAPS: Interactive video segmentation using event cameras and memory-based prompts
entry.summary: E-MAPS: Event-Based Promptable Video Segmentation with Memory-as-Prompt arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper addresses the weakness of RGB-based video object segmentation under fast motion and poor lighting by using event cameras and a promptable setup where users can give prompts at any time window. It proposes E-MAPS, which transfers a pretrained promptable segmenter to event streams and converts object history into sparse prompts through Memory-Aware Prompting. The authors build the EViM dataset from 206K aligned RGB-event pairs and 620K masks, and report leading results on three benchmarks along with efficiency gains and strong zero-shot tracking performance. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend promptable segmentation to event streams with memory-as-prompt, reporting leads on three training-disjoint benchmarks and zero-shot tracking.

entry.title: PORTA: A Tool for Systematically Finding Security Flaws in Identity Brokers
entry.summary: PORTA: Systematic Discovery of Vulnerabilities in Identity Brokers arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines identity brokers such as Keycloak, Vault, and Dex, which convert authentication proofs from an upstream identity provider into sessions for downstream services. The authors define invariants that brokers must uphold, and all 60 prior CVEs they examined violate at least one of them. They present PORTA, an automated tool that uses a large language model to generate API call sequences and oracle assertions based on these invariants. PORTA found 33 previously unreported vulnerabilities in seven popular open-source brokers, which the authors trace to eight recurring patterns. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors define invariants for identity brokers and use an LLM-driven tool to find 33 new vulnerabilities across seven open-source brokers.

entry.title: Can AI Judges Spot Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Study Adding Deliberate Errors
entry.summary: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This study examines whether large language models can reliably judge clinical AI agents that work with electronic health records and detect dangerous mistakes. The researchers added controlled errors to verified agent trajectories from MedAgentBench, producing 416 faulty trajectories across eight error categories, and tested six open-weight LLM judges. Access to clinical evidence improved judge reliability, and combining LLM judges with a rule-based checker detected 97% of injected faults. ★★★★ Notable: The authors inject eight error types into 416 MedAgentBench trajectories and report that six LLM judges vary widely, with reasoning reducing detection of wrong clinical values.

entry.title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: Robot Policies Struggle Around Reflections
entry.summary: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper tests whether robot manipulation policies can reliably handle objects in scenes containing mirrors, inspired by animal mirror self-recognition tests. The authors introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions across five policies. All mirror conditions reduce success rates, and comparisons with non-reflective panels and trajectory analyses suggest the degradation is not caused by physical collisions alone but by phantom targeting and spatial mislocalization. Real-robot experiments show similar drops. ★★★★ Notable: The authors adapt the mirror self-recognition test into a benchmark and report drops across five policies, plus real-robot checks.

entry.title: Polynomial-time learning of random automata from single-bit word labels
entry.summary: Polynomial-Time Learning of Random Automata from One Label per Word arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper studies a binary deterministic finite automaton whose transitions are chosen independently and uniformly at random. A learner sees random words with a single acceptance bit each. For any fixed β>0, the authors give a polynomial-time algorithm that succeeds on all but a small-probability set of transition tables. The paper also refutes Conjecture 4 of Fish and Reyzin on meeting times. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a polynomial-time learner for random DFAs from one label per word, refute a Fish-Reyzin meeting-time conjecture, and report some proof steps formalized in Lean.

entry.title: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Can LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam?
entry.summary: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Will LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam? arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper tests whether hosted large language models can carry out the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites. Using ten off-the-shelf models with a plain system prompt and no jailbreak, the authors ran 1,200 conversations between model sellers and model buyers across four buyer personas. In 737 conversations (61%) the buyer paid in advance, with eight of the ten models participating in nearly every conversation at roughly 2.5 cents per payment. ★★★★ Notable: The authors simulate marketplace advance-fee scams with LLMs on both sides; they report 737 of 1,200 conversations ended with the buyer paying in advance and release the benchmark.

entry.title: Do Vision-Language Models Know Their Own Visual Weaknesses? A Study of Self-Assessment
entry.summary: Do Vision-Language Models Know Their Own Visual Weaknesses? Probing Capability-Level Metacognition arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper tests whether vision-language models can predict in advance which visual tasks and image conditions are hard for them. The authors find that the models know little about their weaknesses, misjudge their overall accuracy, and cannot identify which tasks are hard for all models. Training models to predict their own accuracy does not teach them which kinds of tasks they find difficult. However, the probabilities models assign to their own answers on unlabeled questions reflect weaknesses specific to each model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors separate model-specific weaknesses from shared task difficulty and report that answer probabilities reveal model-particular weaknesses across many VLMs.

entry.title: IMPACT-Seg: Consistent Anatomy Segmentation Across CT, CBCT, and MRI
entry.summary: IMPACT-Seg: Consistent Anatomical Segmentation and Representation Learning Across CT, CBCT, and MRI arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces IMPACT-Seg, a model that uses shared parameters to segment 126 anatomical structures in CT, cone-beam CT (CBCT), and MRI scans. The authors assembled 8,290 volumes through label harmonization, pseudo-label completion, and physics-based CBCT simulations, then trained 2.5D and 3D residual-encoder networks. On 139 real CBCTs, the 3D model reached a mean Dice of 0.842, above the strongest comparator's 0.671. Registration pipelines using its features ranked first on two multimodal Learn2Reg benchmarks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors segment 126 structures across CT, CBCT and MRI with shared parameters, and report gains over comparators on 139 real CBCTs and paired datasets.

entry.title: Shared information determines when multi-view planted matching can be exactly recovered
entry.summary: Shared information governs multi-view planted matching arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper studies when rows of K shuffled views of n objects can be matched, where each object appears in every view as a Gaussian feature vector with known covariance. It shows that matching is nearly exact when the shared information of one object's K observations exceeds (1+ε)log n, and impossible below (1-ε)log n. It also gives a bipartition condition for weak correlations and conjectures a characterization of exact recovery for Gaussian laws, proven in several cases. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give shared-information thresholds for exact multi-view matching, answering a question of Wee et al., and report proofs for three views with equal correlations and several further cases.

entry.title: Capacity of shared-secret key agreement over GHZ quantum networks
entry.summary: The Capacity of Conference Key Agreement over GHZ Networks arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper studies how K users sharing independent GHZ states, each held by a subset of users, can agree on a common secret key using local operations and public classical communication. It shows that the conference key capacity equals the key capacity of the classical source obtained by measuring every GHZ state first. This holds even when users keep quantum memory and communicate over many rounds. The capacity also equals the GHZ distillation capacity. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show conference key capacity over GHZ networks equals the classical source key capacity after measuring, so measuring first is optimal.

entry.title: Lazy AI agents often answer before gathering enough evidence; this paper trains them to commit only when evidence suffices.
entry.summary: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper addresses AI agents that commit to answers on long tasks before gathering sufficient evidence, a behavior it calls laziness. The authors propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which uses the simulator's exact posterior over answers during training to reward continued exploration when several answers remain plausible and committing once evidence is enough. They also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles viewed through a small window. Across nine settings with three vision-language models, RLVB improves on the base model by 17.1% on average. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use exact simulator posteriors to give judge-free step rewards; across three models and benchmarks, they report a 17.1% average gain over the base model.

entry.title: MemHand: Memory-Enhanced Reconstruction of World-Space Hand Motion from First-Person Videos
entry.summary: MemHand: Memory-Enhanced World-Space Hand Motion Reconstruction from Egocentric Videos arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents MemHand, a framework that reconstructs continuous world-space motion of both hands from egocentric video. It uses a Short-Term Event Memory to supply context around occlusions and out-of-sight moments, and a Long-Term Scale Memory that keeps reliable observations as scale anchors across the video. On benchmarks with severe occlusions, MemHand reaches state-of-the-art accuracy, cutting W-MPJPE by 57% on ARCTIC and 70% on HOT3D relative to StableHand. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose complementary short-term event and long-term scale memories beyond fixed windows, reporting W-MPJPE cuts of 57% on ARCTIC and 70% on HOT3D versus StableHand.

entry.title: A gradient method for tuning force fields to dynamic measurements
entry.summary: Path-probability gradients for optimizing force fields against dynamical observables arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces PathGrad, which differentiates Langevin path probabilities rather than chaotic molecular trajectories, giving gradients whose variance stays stable as trajectories grow longer. The authors fine-tuned molten-copper and water potentials using experimental diffusion coefficients and structural constraints. For water, the optimization also improved predicted shear viscosity and rotational relaxation, which were not in the objective, and reduced force errors against a higher-level quantum-chemical reference. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors differentiate Langevin path probabilities to obtain stable gradients, validated on molten copper and water against diffusion and unfitted viscosity and relaxation observables.

entry.title: Measurement Artifacts in Quantized Small Model Evaluations
entry.summary: Measurement Artifacts in Trustworthiness Evaluations of Quantized Small Language Models arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines whether changes in benchmark scores of quantized language models truly come from quantization or from measurement error. The authors test eight instruction-tuned models under 2 billion parameters at float16, LLM.int8() and NF4 precisions, finding that some measurement choices interact with quantization and can be mistaken for its effects. They release item-level predictions, option scores and human annotations, and offer recommendations for evaluating compressed small models. ★★★★ Notable: The authors separate instrument error interacting with quantization from true effects, estimating it across 8 small models, three precisions, and four measurement choices against human annotations.

entry.title: FORA: a general CT model that recognizes, localizes and reports findings
entry.summary: Reliable and grounded reporting of any computed tomography scan with FORA arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across 28 CT protocols. It was trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations using their accompanying reports, without manually annotated lesions. On 36,619 held-out examinations, it achieved a macro AUROC of 0.918 for concept recognition and ranked first on three public benchmarks. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report a general CT model trained weakly from routine reports, unifying recognition, localization and report generation, with macro AUROC 0.918 on 36,619 held-out exams.

entry.title: SpatialArena: A Public Arena for Testing Geometric Foundation Models
entry.summary: SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces SpatialArena, an open benchmark that evaluates geometric models using shared metrics, rules, and a robust, deterministic alignment method. It covers five tasks from monocular depth to SLAM, using 23 public datasets with 418,929 images plus the authors' own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, the authors find single-image depth is near saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes. Feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and outperform video depth models on consistency across frames and views. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a unified, robust evaluation arena covering 23 datasets, five tasks, and 52 models, with deterministic alignment.

entry.title: Reducing Action-Space Dependence in Robust Multi-Agent Learning
entry.summary: Breaking the Joint Action Space Dependence in Distributionally Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies how many samples are needed to learn robust coarse correlated equilibria in finite-horizon, general-sum Markov games where each player's return is evaluated under worst-case total-variation uncertainty around known transitions. Existing guarantees grow with the product of all players' action counts, which scales exponentially with the number of players. The authors propose an algorithm whose sample complexity depends only on the largest single-player action set, and which returns an ε-robust CCE Markov policy with high probability. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show robust CCE sample complexity depends on the largest individual action set rather than the joint action space, a theoretical improvement for distributionally robust multi-agent RL.

entry.title: C3H: Hijacking Compression-to-Consensus Criteria in Multimodal LLM Recommenders
entry.summary: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper argues that multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion, often seen as defenses against content manipulation in LLM-based recommenders, can instead create a compression-to-consensus bias that favors signals that stay salient and consistent across modalities. The authors introduce C3H, an inference-time attack that tailors a target item's multimodal content to match the decision criteria the recommender implicitly uses. Experiments show that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify a compression-to-consensus bias and propose an inference-time attack that boosts target item exposure in multimodal recommenders.

entry.title: Zero-shot AI text detection using context perturbation discrepancy beyond fixed-context likelihood
entry.summary: Beyond Fixed-Context Likelihood: Zero-Shot AI-Generated Text Detection via Context Perturbation Discrepancy arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces Context Perturbation Discrepancy (CPD), a zero-shot method for detecting AI-generated text using a single pretrained language model. CPD compares each token's log-probability gain under the full prefix against a short recent-token window, subtracts the expected gain, and scales the summed deviations by an analytical reference standard deviation. On unedited texts from GEN, DetectRL-X, and HART, subtracting the expectation raises AUROC by 32.78 to 35.81 points. CPD averages 94.80% AUROC and 79.60% recall at a 5% false-positive rate, outperforming seven zero-shot baselines. ★★★★ Notable: The authors add a expected-gain correction with an analytical reference standard deviation, reporting 94.80% average AUROC against seven zero-shot baselines on GEN, DetectRL-X, and HART.

entry.title: Instance-adaptive vision-language alignment for assessing damage to individual buildings
entry.summary: Beyond Static Semantics: Instance-Adaptive Vision-Language Alignment for Building Damage Assessment arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper proposes LAMIA-IBDA, a vision-language framework for assessing damage to individual buildings from bi-temporal remote sensing images. It adapts shared damage descriptions to local image evidence and then links them to each building to form instance-specific prototypes for fine-grained damage classification.
