entry.title: Effect of structured noise on bosonic quantum error correction: how environmental noise can reshape photon-loss errors.
entry.summary: Impact of structured noise on bosonic quantum error correction arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper reports experiments in a three-dimensional circuit quantum electrodynamics system, injecting spectrally engineered environmental noise into a weakly nonlinear oscillator. The measured Fock-state dynamics show clear frequency selectivity, with long-time transition rates converging to the Markovian limit while transient dynamics are non-Markovian, in quantitative agreement with a second-order time-convolutionless theory. Applying narrowband noise to a binomially encoded logical qubit, the authors demonstrate Fock-state-dependent dissipation channels that drive logical states beyond the nominally correctable error space. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report Fock-state-dependent photon loss from structured noise, matching a second-order TCL theory and driving binomially encoded logical states beyond the correctable error space.

entry.title: Expressivity of Observables in Fixed-Readout Quantum Neural Networks
entry.summary: Observable-Level Expressivity in Fixed-Readout Quantum Neural Networks arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper studies which effective observables a quantum neural network with a fixed readout can realize, comparing three physical resource classes: unitary, mixed-unitary, and completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) evolution. The authors show the reachable sets are strictly nested. They give an amplitude-damping example lying outside the mixed-unitary level and derive closed-form loss floors for each level. ★★★★ Notable: The authors characterize reachable effective observables by physical resource class, giving strict inclusions and closed-form loss floors reproduced numerically, plus structured and classification exp

entry.title: Experiment distributing entanglement between atoms at 500 Hz over city-scale fiber
entry.summary: 500 Hz atom-atom entanglement distribution over metropolitan-scale fibers arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper reports an experiment that distributes entanglement between remote atoms over 20 km of optical fiber using two 15 by 15 quantum memory arrays. It generates matter-matter entanglement at 546 Hz without active phase stabilization. The authors state this rate exceeds two-photon and single-photon schemes by factors of 75,932 and 23, and argue the method combines efficiency and robustness for multiplexed quantum repeaters. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report 546 Hz remote atom-atom entanglement over 20 km fiber using two 15×15 quantum memory arrays, unifying efficiency and robustness.

entry.title: Energy limit when replicating fragments in PQG reduced-density-matrix theory
entry.summary: The replication-energy limit of PQG reduced-density-matrix theory from a single-fragment semidefinite program arXiv · Nov 23, 2026The paper studies a size-extensivity problem in variational two-electron reduced-density-matrix calculations, where the energy per fragment can decrease when identical noninteracting fragments are replicated. For the PQG conditions, the authors show that the energy per fragment converges to the minimum of a semidefinite program on a single fragment. The analysis also covers monotonicity in replica count and the role of local electron-number variance, with examples including Be, CH4, N2, H2O and a four-site Hubbard fragment. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove the PQG per-fragment energy limit equals a single-fragment SDP minimum, reached at finite replica count; examples include molecules and a Hubbard fragment.

entry.title: What quantum networks can guarantee about the entangled pairs they deliver
entry.summary: What can a quantum network promise about the entangled pairs it delivers? arXiv · Nov 23, 2026Quantum networks deliver entangled qubit pairs, but users cannot measure each pair's fidelity without destroying it, so networks usually promise quality based on a physical model. The paper shows that secretly testing some pairs at random lets users bound the average fidelity of the pairs they keep without relying on a model. Testing only a small fraction, however, cannot reliably guarantee that every kept pair meets a threshold. The authors give a rule that limits the risk of receiving a bad pair, provided the model is not overly optimistic or a sufficient margin is declared in advance. ★★★★ Notable: The authors separate average from per-pair fidelity guarantees, giving a model-free average lower bound and a model-conditional per-pair risk bound; the abstract reports validation on a 36-qubit trapp

entry.title: Local redundancies are necessary for long-lived memories in finite spatial dimensions
entry.summary: Local redundancies are necessary for long-lived memories in finite spatial dimensions arXiv · Nov 23, 2026The paper proves a no-go theorem against exponentially long-lived thermal memories, based on redundancies among Hamiltonian terms. For local stabilizer Hamiltonians without local redundancies, it shows that at any constant nonzero temperature, local heat-bath dynamics mixes fast, with O(N) mixing time, where N is the number of qubits. Under a stronger condition on induced redundancies, it proves rapid mixing with O(log N) mixing time. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that without local redundancies, heat-bath dynamics mixes fast, with O(log N) mixing time shown under stronger redundancy conditions, including Haah's cubic code.

entry.title: Tighter upper limits on two-way capacity for amplitude-damping quantum channels
entry.summary: Improved two-way capacity upper bounds for amplitude-damping channels arXiv · Nov 23, 2026The paper gives an improved upper bound, log₂[1+(1-γ)γ^{γ/(1-γ)}], on the two-way-assisted capacities of the qubit amplitude-damping channel with decay probability γ. The bound applies to quantum communication, entanglement distribution, private communication and secret-key agreement. The authors extend sector teleportation simulation to qubits and determine the exact additive relative entropy of entanglement of amplitude-damping resources. They also derive explicit bounds for generalized amplitude damping, which includes thermal excitation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive an improved two-way capacity upper bound for amplitude-damping channels, extending sector teleportation simulation to qubits and reporting strict gains over known bounds.

entry.title: How phase rigidity scales with system size without eigenstate merging
entry.summary: Scaling of phase rigidity without eigenstate coalescence arXiv · Nov 22, 2026The paper studies how non-Hermitian skin effects determine the way phase rigidity changes with system size, without any eigenstate coalescence. Exact analytical results are derived for three non-Hermitian chain models and checked numerically. Phase rigidity decays exponentially under the ordinary skin effect, approaches a nonzero constant as N^-2 under the scale-free skin effect, and can decay as N^-1/2 to zero under the algebraic skin effect. These results show that eigenstate nonorthogonality can be controlled without exceptional points. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show skin effects give distinct phase-rigidity scaling without eigenstate coalescence, reporting exact results for three chain models with numerical checks.

entry.title: Generalized second law derived from fluctuation theorems in a quantum reference frame
entry.summary: The Generalized Second Law from Fluctuation Theorems in a Quantum Reference Frame arXiv · Nov 22, 2026This paper proves the generalized second law (GSL) for black-hole exteriors undergoing unitary driving and relaxation on a fixed semifinite algebra. Instead of Wall's approach, which assumes semiclassical geometry and restricts to algebras of successive horizon cuts, it evolves the state on a fixed dressed exterior algebra and uses a gravitational charge as a quantum clock. The authors formulate the GSL through a quantum channel fluctuation theorem, giving three complementary versions. They establish entropy bounds that yield the GSL in a slow-clock limit and quantify finite-width clock corrections. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use a gravitational charge as a quantum clock to build a modular crossed product and derive the GSL via a channel fluctuation theorem, with bounds in a slow-clock limit.

entry.title: Undecidable quantum storage: whether a fixed circuit keeps quantum information cannot be determined from noise rate alone
entry.summary: Undecidable quantum storage: no algorithm can tell from the noise rate whether a fixed circuit remembers arXiv · Nov 22, 2026The paper constructs fixed local quantum circuits for which no algorithm can determine, from the noise rate alone, whether the circuit can store a qubit for a long time under one-dimensional single-qubit noise. Disjoint rate intervals are indexed by inputs to a universal Turing machine: if the machine runs forever, a qubit is stored for a time growing with system size, while if it halts, fidelity drops below a fixed bound. These are existence results with very large system sizes and very small noise rates. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors build fixed local circuits from a universal Turing machine so that noise rate alone cannot decide storage, with encoding and decoding maps giving storage and failure results.

entry.title: Total information from pairs of alternative quantum measurements, bounded by Holevo information
entry.summary: Holevo-Bounded Total Information from Pair Distributions of Alternative Quantum Measurements arXiv · Nov 21, 2026The paper studies quantum ensembles whose accessible information can be strictly smaller than their Holevo information, and asks whether information spread across two alternative measurement contexts can close this gap without assigning a joint distribution to their outcomes. Building on a relative-entropy projection method by Harder et al., it defines a directed posterior novelty for each record and an associated total-information quantity. For finite-dimensional classical-quantum ensembles, it proves that optimizing this quantity over pairs of POVMs yields a value between the accessible and Holevo information. ★★★★ Notable: The authors define a pair-measurement total-information quantity bounded between accessible and Holevo information, saturating Holevo on BB84, and settle quantum validity of an information causality c

entry.title: Modern self-supervised vision transformers show pareidolia, seeing patterns in noise
entry.summary: Modern Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Are Pareidolic arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper finds that some self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) form spatially coherent patterns across patches even on white noise, a behavior the authors call pareidolia, with the related directions forming a pareidolic subspace. On natural images this subspace holds most feature variance in DINOv2 and DINOv3 but little in DINO, which the authors link to those models' weaker object emergence. They propose Pareidolia Subspace Calibration (PSC), a training-free method that scales down these directions, and report gains on object discovery, saliency detection, and video object segmentation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify a pareidolic subspace in self-supervised ViTs and propose a training-free calibration, reporting gains across object discovery, saliency, and video segmentation.

entry.title: CTLink: A Text-Prompted Model Linking Chest CT Report Findings to Scan Regions
entry.summary: CTLink: A Text-Prompted Segmentation Model for Linking Radiology Report Findings to 3D Chest CT Scans arXiv · Nov 24, 2026Radiology reports describe findings only in text, so readers cannot see on the scan which abnormality each finding refers to. CTLink is a text-prompted 3D segmentation model that outlines the findings described in a chest CT report. It was trained on 4123 noncontrast chest CT scans with 9547 segmented findings, including the newly annotated ReXGroundingCTv2 dataset. On validation scans it outperformed the public model VoxTell, and it achieved the highest hit rate and instance F1 among 48 teams in the MICCAI 2026 ReXGrounding challenge. ★★★★ Notable: The authors link report findings to 3D chest CT segmentation with a new annotated dataset, reporting gains over VoxTell and matching inter-rater agreement.

entry.title: Checking PDE solver outputs, from finite elements to neural surrogates
entry.summary: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper proposes that solvers return a certificate with their answers, which a small independent checker converts into guaranteed error bounds against a written physics specification. The authors apply this checker to outputs from FEniCSx, solvers written by large language models, and neural surrogate models. The certificate rejects several plausible buggy solutions that pass standard grid convergence tests. For neural surrogates, it yields valid per-prediction bounds that are very narrow inside the training range and much wider outside it. The bounds are informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply an independent certificate checker to any PDE solver output, including LLM-written code and neural surrogates, on a cardiac ablation problem, reporting five injected bugs and three L

entry.title: Matching Under Metric Privacy: Accurate Private-Public Point Matching While Protecting Locations
entry.summary: Matching Under Metric Privacy arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper studies how to represent and randomize points in d-dimensional Euclidean space so that bipartite matchings between private and public points stay accurate under metric privacy. It analyzes local mechanisms and a Gumbel matching method for cases where a trusted server receives the private points. The authors establish a tight rate of Θ(n·min{d, log n}/ε) for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum, and benchmark experiments suggest d ≈ log n as a practical transition point. ★★★★ Notable: The authors establish a tight rate Θ(n·min{d,log n}/ε) for metric-private matching and propose Gumbel matching, with upper bounds, worst-case constructions, and benchmark experiments reported.

entry.title: Decoupling Faults from Uncertainty: Message-Efficient Byzantine Agreement with Local Predictions
entry.summary: Decoupling Faults from Uncertainty: Message-Efficient Byzantine Agreement with Local Predictions arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies how much Byzantine Agreement can benefit when each process has a local bound on its failure-prediction error. It introduces a local k-error prediction model and presents a synchronous algorithm requiring n ≥ t + 4k + 1. When local uncertainty is small, the protocol's communication is decoupled from the total fault budget t, achieving o(n²) communication when t = Θ(n) and k = o(√n). The authors also show that at least Ω(nk) honest messages are necessary in this model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a local k-error prediction model, give a Byzantine agreement protocol with o(n²) communication, and report a matching Ω(nk) lower bound.

entry.title: SPROUT: Predicting Which Text Prompts Most Improve Text-to-Image Model Tuning
entry.summary: SPROUT: Predicting Objective-Grounded Prompt Utility for Efficient Text-to-Image Preference Tuning arXiv · Nov 24, 2026Preference tuning of text-to-image diffusion models spends much compute generating candidate images, while training prompts are usually sampled at random. SPROUT predicts each prompt's utility with a text-only model that is refit after every iteration, then uses a randomized acceptance rule to form training batches without generating extra images. Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 1.5 with DGPO on GenEval, SPROUT matches uniform sampling's final score in about 44% of iterations and beats both uniform sampling and CGPO on the learning-curve area. ★★★★ Notable: The authors predict prompt gradient-norm utility with a text-only model to select tuning prompts, reporting efficiency gains on GenEval and other benchmarks.

entry.title: Optimal regret lower bounds for learning in matrix games
entry.summary: Optimal Regret Lower Bounds in Matrix Games arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper studies learning in two-player zero-sum matrix games, where players with m and n actions choose mixed strategies over T rounds. It proves that for every deterministic learning dynamic there is a payoff matrix whose maximum individual regret is Ω(√(log m log n)), which matches the known upper bound. The paper also establishes a lower bound of Ω(min{T, log min{m, n}}) for all m, n, and T, using an adaptive construction of the payoff matrix. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give regret lower bounds matching known upper bounds for deterministic dynamics in matrix games, via an adaptive rank-one payoff construction.

entry.title: FATCAT: Physical fault attacks that disable chip-level model alignment
entry.summary: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents FATCAT, a physical fault-injection attack that can stop large language and vision-language models from refusing malicious prompts. It uses non-invasive electromagnetic fault injection on GPU-accelerated systems-on-chip, with a radio-frequency side-channel trigger that times the faults to the prompt prefill phase and corrupts memory transactions. The attack was tested on NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor with Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, and was also shown to cause hazardous movements in a robotic arm controlled by a SmolVLA policy. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first electromagnetic fault-injection attack removing LLM refusals, reporting Jetson experiments and a robotic-arm demonstration of physical harm.

entry.title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents: Rewriting Own Weights from Experience Between Tasks, Without Training
entry.summary: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper introduces a self-upgrading embodied agent that learns from its own experience by rewriting one tensor of its weights between tasks, with no training, gradients, reward model, or second model. It finds wasted steps in its outputs, traces the habit to a direction in its hidden states, and tests each edit against its unchanged self, keeping only edits that hold. The authors report that a 27B agent, after one kept edit, completes significantly more tasks in fewer steps with fewer wasted outputs and tokens across thousands of held-out episodes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report an embodied agent that rewrites one weight tensor between tasks without training, self-testing edits, with gains over thousands of held-out episodes.

entry.title: AI Coding Assistants and Tech Hiring: How GitHub Copilot Affects Labor Demand
entry.summary: AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies how firms adopted GitHub Copilot, an AI coding assistant, across 5,414 multinational firms that account for 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. The authors use firms' predetermined software procurement cycles as a natural experiment to identify causal effects. After one year, adoption reduced quarterly technical hiring by 29%, with no effect on separations or overall technical headcount. The slowdown is concentrated in junior technical roles with the most coding work, and firms shift demand toward more experienced workers and roles combining coding with broader design responsibilities. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors use a natural experiment across 5,414 firms to causally estimate AI coding assistants' effect on technical hiring, with broad labor-market implications.

entry.title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM agents rebuild efficient circuits from pin-level experiments?
entry.summary: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments? arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents ChiProgramBench, 18 hardware tasks drawn from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden simulated reference circuit and must submit a gate-level netlist built from public library cells. The benchmark runs 432 trials across black-box discovery and function-guided reconstruction settings. Only 12.0% and 14.8% of trials, respectively, pass every hidden test case, and only three of the 58 fully passing designs beat the reference on combined power, area, and delay. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a pin-level benchmark for rebuilding gate-level circuits and report 432 trials showing behavioral recovery lags efficient implementation.

entry.title: Déjà VAE: When Autoencoder Traces Reveal Generated Images
entry.summary: Déjà VAE: When Do Autoencoder Traces Reveal Generated Images? arXiv · Nov 24, 2026Latent diffusion model outputs already pass through their autoencoder, so a second round trip changes them very little, a effect underlying reconstruction-based detectors of generated images. The paper analyses when this trace reveals a generated image and when it does not, using frozen vision foundation models and experiments on Synthbuster, GenImage and Chameleon. It also finds that benchmark protocols, such as how real photographs are matched to generated images, can change which detector appears stronger. ★★★★ Notable: The authors analyse when autoencoder round-trip traces reveal generated images, validating on Synthbuster and GenImage and flagging benchmark protocol sensitivity.

entry.title: Black-box comparator-adaptive network regret: analyzing regret in decentralized online learning and a general reduction method
entry.summary: Black-Box Comparator-Adaptive Network Regret arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies decentralized online learning, where each node's predictions are judged by their loss across the whole network (network regret). The authors show that existing gossip-based algorithms cannot achieve sublinear network regret with one gossip step per round, using a two-node counterexample where regret grows exponentially. They then propose a black-box reduction in which nodes exchange predictions with neighbors once per round, using edge weights that work on any connected undirected graph and achieve sublinear regret. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show gossip methods can incur exponential network regret, propose a black-box reduction, and report experiments on synthetic and real data.

entry.title: Accurate Products, Inaccurate Inverse: Emulated FP64 Matrix Operations in Triangular Inversion
entry.summary: Accurate Products, Inaccurate Inverse: Emulated FP64 BLAS in Blocked Triangular Inversion arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper asks whether a blocked triangular inversion built from emulated FP64 matrix products keeps the accuracy of those products. The authors find that every product meets the standard error bound, yet the computed inverse is far less accurate than native FP64, because one product's summed index carries both a diagonal scaling and its inverse. Computing the problematic products natively restores accuracy, and the paper also presents equilibration, a solve-based reformulation, and an error recurrence for auditing runs. Speed comparisons on an RTX 4090 are included. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show per-product accuracy does not carry over to blocked triangular inversion, identify the culprit product, and report validation on four GPUs and real covariance matrices.

entry.title: Can hidden reasoning steer LLM outputs without leaving a visible trace?
entry.summary: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace? arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper asks whether large language models can complete multi-step reasoning entirely internally, outputting only a final answer. The authors show that a simple auxiliary loss lets models solve a multi-step task latently at least 5x deeper than previously reported. In loan decision and code generation tasks, a model trained to pursue a hidden objective produced chain-of-thought explanations with no trace of that objective, and a strong LLM monitor did not flag it. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show latent reasoning can be at least 5x deeper than reported and build models with hidden objectives invisible in CoT, testing loan decisions and code generation.

entry.title: Regression with pseudo-labels calibrated by labeled data, beyond standard minimax limits
entry.summary: Prediction-Powered Regression via Calibration: Beyond the Supervised Minimax Benchmark arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies nonparametric regression when labeled data are scarce but many observations come with possibly inaccurate pseudo-labels. The proposed method, wPPRC, first calibrates pseudo-labels using labeled data and then fits a predictor by weighted regression on observed and calibrated responses. Over Hölder classes, the authors derive nonasymptotic excess-risk bounds for clipped ReLU estimators and a matching minimax lower bound up to logarithmic factors under suitable conditions. They also propose a validation-selected estimator that chooses the weight using an independent labeled sample, and illustrate the gains through simulations and an application to predicting homeless counts. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a calibrated pseudo-label weighted regression, derive near-matching minimax bounds on Hölder classes, and report improvements over four baselines with simulations and a homelessnes

entry.title: Aggregation rules that KL-regularised preference learning on networks produces
entry.summary: Aggregation Rules Induced by KL-Regularised Preference Dynamics on Networks arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper studies agents that each align a model to their own preference data while observing one another, asking which aggregation rule the resulting policies implement. It analyses cases where the reference and challenger are each either the agent's own preference or an average over observed agents. With a fixed challenger the rule is cardinal, while aggregating both yields an ordinal rule, the collective policy being a maximal lottery up to a bounded slack. ★★★★ Notable: The authors link KL-regularised preference dynamics with network attention, deriving cardinal and ordinal collective aggregation rules and characterising their weights, with results reported across re

entry.title: Optimal matroid prophet inequality against all-knowing adversaries, and delegation
entry.summary: Optimal Matroid Prophets against Almighty Adversaries and Delegation arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper proves an optimal one-half matroid prophet inequality against an almighty adversary who sees all realized values before choosing the arrival order. The algorithm is deterministic: before values are revealed it partitions the ground set, replaces the matroid with a stricter direct sum of minors, fixes one threshold per part, and accepts greedily under these tests. The same construction yields a deterministic, agent-oblivious mechanism for matroid delegation with possibly correlated agent utilities, improving the guarantee from 1/4 to the optimal 1/2. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give a deterministic optimal 1/2 matroid prophet inequality against almighty adversaries, improving matroid delegation to 1/2 with tight bounds.

entry.title: Hidden Supply-Chain Risks in LLM Agent Skills, From Inherited Dependencies to Agent-Specific Flaws
entry.summary: Carried-Over and Agent-Native Threats in the Supply Chain of LLM Agent Skills arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper empirically studies security flaws in 48,682 agent skills on ClawHub, focusing on vulnerabilities that skill authors introduce unintentionally. It examines four risk types: dependencies, first-party code, install instructions, and credentials printed to stdout. The authors combine static analysis, manual review, sandbox execution, and tests with a live LLM agent under indirect prompt injection to check whether these flaws can actually be reached. Many skills depend on vulnerable versions at publication, yet few of those vulnerabilities are reachable from agent input, while most sampled first-party flaws were exploitable in the sandbox. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a registry-scale study of all 48,682 ClawHub skills, testing reachability of flaws in a sandbox and with a live agent under injection.

entry.title: PRIMEAPE: A Multilingual Benchmark for Detailed Evaluation of Judge Models
entry.summary: PRIMEAPE: A Multilingual Benchmark for Fine-Grained Meta-Evaluation of Judge Models arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper introduces PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating how well judge models' verdicts and rationales match human preferences. It contains 2,205 response pairs for 243 instructions in seven languages, with 11k human annotations across several criteria. The authors find that a judge can give reasons consistent with its verdict while still disagreeing with humans, so internal consistency does not guarantee alignment with human judgment. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a multilingual benchmark of 2,205 pairs in seven languages with 11k human annotations, reporting that judges' verdict-rationale consistency does not guarantee human alignment.

entry.title: TrialAgentBench: A Benchmark Testing AI Agents on Clinical Trial Analysis and Long-Term Drug Development Decisions
entry.summary: TrialAgentBench: Evaluating AI Agents for Clinical-Trial Analysis and Long-Horizon Drug-Development Decisions arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper introduces TrialAgentBench, a benchmark for testing how well AI agents analyse clinical trials and make drug development decisions. It uses simulated trials with known outcomes and publicly releases nearly 3,500 tasks, from single-trial analysis to multi-phase programmes with budget and time limits. The strongest agents analyse messy trial data closely, but they struggle with decisions under uncertainty and reach only about 48% of the value an oracle achieves on drug programmes. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a benchmark using simulated trials with known truth, evaluating 24 models on nearly 3,500 tasks and reporting their results against oracle baselines.

entry.title: Studying the Detectors That Screen Agent Skill Hubs
entry.summary: Demystifying Detectors Guarding Agent Skill Hubs arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents the first systematic study of six malicious-skill detectors, four adopted by public skill hubs and two community-provided, tested on 1,477 agent skills from seven datasets. The best-performing detector still misses 4.9% of malicious skills and wrongly flags 17.8% of benign ones. The authors identify two recurring failure causes: flagging sensitive operations without considering their legitimate purpose, and recognizing threats but underrating or dismissing them. Guided by this analysis, they refined the prompts of a state-of-the-art detector, improving its mean F1 score in eight of nine evaluation settings. ★★★★ Notable: The authors systematically evaluate six skill detectors on 1477 skills, identify two failure mechanisms, and report prompt refinements improving F1 in most settings.

entry.title: World Models Used as Native Latent Action Models
entry.summary: World Models as Native Latent Action Models arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper proposes Native LAM, which uses one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both an inverse- and forward-dynamics model, connected only by learnable dynamics registers. Trained on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ only in motion, it distills a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. The authors also introduce PAWlicy, a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action policies that uses Native LAM as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors use a pretrained video world model directly as a latent action model with dynamics registers, and report results on LARY, RoboTwin 2.0, and real robots.

entry.title: Proactive Task Assistants Should Judge by Evidence, Not Timing
entry.summary: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper examines how proactive assistants guiding people through physical tasks decide whether each step is complete or a mistake has occurred. The authors find that two benchmarks largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what, as a timer that ignores the video scores highly. They introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training, which pairs positives and negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time. A 2B model trained this way surpasses the timing-only frontier on both benchmarks and distinguishes finished from unfinished steps at equal elapsed time. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show timer-only policies beat published results on Ego-MC-Bench, then propose Evidence-Contrastive Training, reporting gains over that frontier on both benchmarks across four seeds.

entry.title: Vitrify Exact Learning: finding exact differential equations and closed forms from numerical data
entry.summary: Vitrify Exact Learning: exact differential equations, changes of variable and closed forms from numerical data arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents Vitrify Exact Learning, a method that takes numerical values of a function and assumes it is annihilated by a linear differential operator with polynomial coefficients. It finds that operator from weak-form integral measurements, verifies it on held-out data against a propagated noise level, then solves it symbolically to keep a matching closed form. On noise-free benchmarks it recovers more targets than the compared programs, but with noise in several variables, sparse data, or equations above fourth order it mostly returns no model. ★★★★ Notable: Combines weak-form null-vector operator recovery, exact coefficients, noise testing and symbolic solving to recover closed forms; the authors report higher success counts than other programs on severa

entry.title: KL divergence should never be negative, yet PyTorch sometimes returns negative values
entry.summary: The KL Divergence Is Never Negative, Except in PyTorch arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper notes that Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence is mathematically never negative, yet PyTorch users have reported negative values for years, usually handled by clamping to zero. The authors test 18 closed-form KL families and F.kl_div on millions of inputs and find widespread value and gradient errors on CPU and GPU. They propose stable closed-form decompositions, compensated arithmetic, and analytic gradients, which remove most significant errors. The authors report that the repaired code largely eliminates the errors' effects on downstream tasks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors expose systematic numerical failures of common KL divergence implementations on nearby distributions, proposing stable decompositions and compensated arithmetic, validated on 8.5 million i

entry.title: Exact asymptotic theory for non-convex M-estimators in high-dimensional statistics
entry.summary: Precise Asymptotics of Non-Convex M-Estimators arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper studies M-estimation in generalized linear models where the loss or regularizer may be non-convex, under rotationally invariant designs in the proportional asymptotic regime. It analyzes the problem with Vector Approximate Message Passing (VAMP), whose iterates are described by a low-dimensional State Evolution recursion. When proximal operators are discontinuous, the authors correct the Onsager terms using a distributional Stein's lemma and prove State Evolution holds for the corrected VAMP. The theory is applied to group sparse regression with an ℓ0-type penalty and to robust regression with the Cauchy loss. ★★★★ Notable: The authors correct VAMP's Onsager terms for discontinuous proximal operators, prove state evolution holds, and apply it to l0 group sparse regression and Cauchy-loss robust regression.

entry.title: How quantum resources limit function approximation
entry.summary: Quantum resources constrain function approximation arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper studies how four quantum resources (coherence, imaginarity, entanglement, and magic) constrain what a quantum learning model can approximate, with a fixed encoding and readout. In a one-qubit phase-encoding model, coherence bounds the oscillation of the model function and imaginarity bounds its odd part. For domains away from zero, Clifford trainable gates suffice for uniform approximation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors link coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic to function-approximation bounds, and report a polynomial Clifford-replacement result for magic.

entry.title: BridgeMVS: Linking Multi-View Stereo and Monocular Depth Estimation
entry.summary: BridgeMVS: Bridging Multi-View Stereo and Monodepth via Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion arXiv · Nov 23, 2026The paper proposes BridgeMVS, a multi-stage framework that connects monocular depth features with multi-view cost volumes through Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion (BDF). Monocular structure guides more robust multi-view depth estimation, while multi-view geometry recalibrates monocular representations for metric-scale consistency. The authors report state-of-the-art results on the DTU, Tanks-and-Temples, and ETH3D benchmarks, with improved monocular depth accuracy and first place on both Tanks-and-Temples Intermediate and Advanced. BDF is designed as a plug-and-play module for existing cascaded MVS frameworks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose bidirectional dynamic fusion linking monocular depth and cost volumes, reporting state-of-the-art results on DTU, Tanks-and-Temples, and ETH3D, as a plug-and-play module.
